purpose: Meropenem is a strong antibiotic used to fight serious bacterial infections in the body. It is commonly used for infections in the lungs, stomach, skin, urinary tract, and brain. Doctors often use it when other antibiotics have not worked or when the infection is severe.
how_it_works: Meropenem works by attacking the outer wall that bacteria need to survive and grow. Think of the bacterial wall like a protective shell — meropenem punches holes in that shell, causing the bacteria to fall apart and die. Because it targets a part that human cells do not have, it kills the bacteria without harming your own body cells.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea are the most common issues. You may also notice redness, swelling, or soreness at the IV site where the medication goes in. Some people get headaches or a mild rash. Let your nurse or doctor know if any of these bother you.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you develop a severe rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or have trouble breathing, as these could be signs of a serious allergic reaction. If you have had a bad reaction to penicillin or other antibiotics before, make sure your doctor knows. This medication may rarely cause seizures, especially if you already have kidney problems or a history of seizures. Do not stop treatment early unless your doctor tells you to, even if you feel better.
typical_dosing: Meropenem is given through an IV (directly into a vein) in a hospital or infusion center — you will not take this one at home as a pill. A typical adult dose is 500 mg to 2 grams given every 6 to 8 hours, depending on how serious your infection is and how well your kidneys are working. Each dose is usually given as a slow drip over 15 to 30 minutes, or sometimes over 3 hours for certain infections. Your doctor will decide the exact dose that is right for you.
